item.title: How Illumine cracked the US SaaS market from India: AI, GTM, Growth playbook
item.description: In this episode of the Prime Venture Partners Podcast, Illumine co-founders Navneet Rastogi and Sourabh Agarwal share how they went from losing nearly 200 customers during COVID to building a global childcare SaaS business, competing with established US players and scaling sales from India.
item.content:encoded:
Three months of advertising on Meta had produced disappointing results for Illumine, an Indian SaaS startup trying to establish itself in the competitive US childcare software market. The founders were close to abandoning the channel when they decided to run one final experiment. Instead of asking prospective customers to sign up immediately, they shifted their campaigns towards building awareness.

The results changed their approach to customer acquisition. Illumine went from generating approximately 20 leads a month to 400–500, with Meta eventually contributing 60–70% of its leads.

"The point was the awareness was not there," says Navneet Rastogi, Co-founder of Illumine.

It was one of several lessons that helped Illumine evolve from a bootstrapped Indian startup into a vertical SaaS platform serving preschools and childcare centres across more than 50 countries. Today, India accounts for less than 15% of its revenue, while the US has become a major focus for the business.

In a conversation with Gaurav Ranjan, Principal at Prime Venture Partners, co-founders Rastogi and Sourabh Agarwal discussed the company's international expansion, its experiments with go-to-market strategies and why customer understanding matters more than sophisticated technology.

From 200 customers to almost zero during COVID

Illumine began with a personal problem. As a parent, Rastogi wanted better visibility into his son's daily experiences at preschool. The founders subsequently discovered that even large childcare chains were struggling with outdated software designed for conventional schools rather than the operational complexities of early childhood education.

Their first customer, one of India's largest premium preschool chains, provided enough revenue for the founders to bootstrap the business. For nearly six months, they worked alongside teachers, administrators and finance teams to understand the workflows before building the product.

But COVID disrupted everything. Illumine had approximately 200 customers before childcare centres began shutting down. Unlike conventional education, childcare could not simply move online.

The crisis forced the founders to explore international markets where centres were still operating. Organic demand from the Middle East and Southeast Asia provided the initial opportunity, with Dubai eventually becoming an important market for the company.

The experience also prepared Illumine for the US. According to Rastogi, approximately 90% of childcare workflows were similar across geographies, with the remaining differences handled through product configuration.

Why Illumine chose Texas and Florida over California

Entering the US presented a different challenge. Established competitors such as Procare had decades of experience, strong customer relationships and substantial market presence.

Rather than following the conventional advice to begin in California, Illumine evaluated states based on three factors: market size, competitive intensity and customer purchasing power. Texas, Florida and New York became its initial focus areas.

The founders also realised that desk research could not replace understanding customers on the ground. During one visit, Rastogi and two colleagues walked approximately 30,000 steps across Manhattan, visiting childcare centres as prospective parents to understand their admissions and operating processes.

A particularly revealing experience came during a small event in Florida. An attendee questioned why customers should trust an unfamiliar Indian company over Procare, which had been operating for more than two decades.

Rastogi responded by asking whether existing providers had listened to customers' requests for improvements. The discussion revealed a simple but underserved requirement: communicating with Spanish-speaking families.

Illumine built the capability, helping it gain traction in Florida.

"Online will tell you the fancy thing to do, but it was not the reality there," Rastogi recalls.

The positioning mistake that was hurting conversions

Illumine's early US marketing attracted enquiries, but many came from small home daycare operators rather than established childcare businesses looking to replace their existing systems.

The founders realised that while their advanced features were attracting attention, they were not necessarily convincing customers to switch.

"Fancy is getting them into the call but not getting them to convert," Rastogi explains.

The team began mapping childcare centres across US states, studying their size, fees, existing software and purchasing power. It also changed how the product was positioned, balancing its AI capabilities with the core operational requirements customers expected from a childcare management platform.

This research informed the company's paid acquisition experiments. Google Ads was already generating leads from customers actively searching for solutions, but Meta was underperforming.

After three unsuccessful months, the team switched from lead-generation campaigns to awareness campaigns. Monthly lead volumes subsequently increased from approximately 20 to 400–500.

Importantly, Rastogi says the company also began attracting higher-value customers through the channel. The lesson was not simply about advertising optimisation. Illumine first needed to establish credibility as a serious alternative to established software providers.

Selling to US customers with a team in India

Illumine's US expansion did not depend on building a large American sales organisation. According to Rastogi, approximately 90% of its US revenue is generated by employees working from India.

However, adapting to American sales expectations required changes in how the team conducted conversations. Unlike Indian sales calls, which often move quickly into business discussions, US customers expected relationship-building, video interactions and a more consultative approach.

The company also recruited people with direct childcare industry experience, including former centre directors, who could speak to customers about their operational challenges rather than merely demonstrate software features.

This approach helped Illumine build trust in a market where customers were understandably cautious about adopting a relatively unfamiliar international platform.

The founders also learnt that implementation capacity had to grow alongside sales. A surge in customer onboarding around September required them to move experienced employees into customer success to support new deployments.

AI that reduces three hours of work to ten minutes

For Illumine, AI adoption has been driven by operational problems rather than the technology itself. Childcare teachers, for instance, spend considerable time documenting activities and sharing updates with parents, often sorting through hundreds of photographs after a full day of managing children.

Agarwal describes how a centre might generate 1,000 photographs daily, requiring teachers to identify children, organise activities and prepare individual parent updates. Illumine's AI now helps automate this process while allowing teachers to review and approve the output.

"So the 3 hours work went to 10 minutes now," Agarwal says.

The company is extending this approach to financial reconciliation, parent communication and front-desk operations. According to Rastogi, AI functionality can be upsold at nearly twice the base software price, creating an additional monetisation opportunity.

But the founders remain cautious about where automation belongs. Illumine declined requests to use AI-powered cameras to analyse children's emotions, preferring to leave observation and decisions involving children to educators.

Why the next SaaS moat is understanding the customer

With AI making software development increasingly accessible, Rastogi believes technology alone is becoming a weaker competitive advantage. What remains difficult to replicate is the accumulated understanding of complex customer workflows, from billing and payroll to occupancy management and regulatory compliance.

For Illumine, this knowledge has been built through years of working directly with childcare operators, including customers whose demanding requirements forced the company to improve its product.

Venture capital has also changed the founders' ambitions. After years of prioritising investments that delivered immediate returns, they could pursue longer-term opportunities and accelerate international expansion.

With the business growing approximately threefold year on year, according to the founders, Illumine is now exploring adjacent revenue opportunities in payments, insurance and compliance. Payments alone could eventually become several times larger than its core software revenue.

For a company that nearly lost its entire customer base during COVID, the ambition has changed considerably. Illumine is no longer simply trying to build better software for preschools. It wants to become one of the largest technology platforms serving the global childcare industry.

As Rastogi puts it, "I see a big opportunity to build."

item.title: Momentum by Google and YourStory to bring India’s founders, investors, and policymakers into one room in New Delhi
item.description: Momentum by Google, in collaboration with YourStory, puts India’s startup future on one stage, with the people who will build, fund, and shape it.
item.content:encoded:
India’s startup story is no longer only about how many companies are being built; it is about how far they can go. The answer increasingly depends on conversations that happen between the people building, funding, and shaping the rules for those companies.

Google, in collaboration with YourStory, is hosting Momentum by Google, an invite-only gathering bringing together leaders from India’s startup ecosystem and innovation economy, on November 23, 2026, in New Delhi.

The evening will bring together a select group of startup founders, technology leaders, venture capital investors, and policy stakeholders around one question: what will it take for India’s innovators to build and scale globally as AI becomes part of every product and every business?

Momentum is a forum where ideas, experience, and perspectives on policy can be exchanged openly and directly. The focus will be on celebrating India’s technological momentum, highlighting emerging innovation, and fostering the collaborative frameworks that digital enterprises need to scale globally.

Who will be in the room?

The keynote on catalyzing India’s next tech leap will be delivered by Amardeep Singh Bhatia, IAS, Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). The audience will also hear from Wilson L. White, Vice President of Government Affairs and Public Policy for Platforms and Devices at Google, who leads government affairs across Asia-Pacific.

The sessions will be led by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, The Bharat Project and YourStory Media. Speakers include Prof. Dr. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, ZenteiQ.ai; Ritu Mehrotra, Founder and CEO, Shunya Labs; Rajesh Ranjan, Director and India Lead for Government Affairs and Public Policy (GAPP) at Google; and Siddharth Shekhar, Director at Google, who oversees Government and PSUs, BFSI, Fintech, Education, and Auto.

What will the conversations cover?

A fireside chat on building and scaling with frontier AI will look at what it means for a startup to build with advanced AI at its core, and what it takes to grow from a promising idea into a company that competes on a global stage. As frontier AI becomes part of how products are designed, built, and taken to market, the conversation will explore how founders can use it to scale.

Frontier AI is also changing what policymakers need to consider. The panel discussion, on driving innovation and policy alignment for India’s AI ecosystem, will bring founders, industry, and government perspectives together to explore how regulation, public policy, and industry can move together. It will look at how policy can support new entrants as well as established players, and how the ecosystem can keep growing responsibly and competitively.

An open Q&A will give the audience an opportunity to engage in dialogue with the speakers and seek their views on the issues shaping India’s startup ecosystem.

Bringing the ecosystem together

Policy and innovation are now part of the same conversation. As AI moves from experimentation to everyday infrastructure, founders are making decisions about how to build, what to invest in, and where to compete, while policymakers are weighing how to encourage growth while keeping the ecosystem responsible and trusted.

Momentum by Google aims to bring founders, technology leaders, investors, and policymakers into the same conversation, with discussions that move from the practical realities of building and scaling with frontier AI to the larger question of how regulation, industry, and entrepreneurship can move in step.

It is also built to be interactive, with room for attendees to engage directly with speakers and bring their own questions and experiences into the conversation. For founders, that means a chance to share what it actually takes to scale a company in India today. For policymakers and investors, it offers a view of the ground realities behind the headlines. It is an exchange that works best when the people on both sides are in the same room.

Why the room matters

India’s startup ecosystem has become a primary engine of the country’s economic and technological transformation, and Momentum by Google reflects a growing recognition that the most meaningful progress often happens when the right people are in the same room and willing to listen to one another.

By convening founders, investors, and policymakers around a shared interest in India’s technological future, Google and YourStory are creating that room in New Delhi. For attendees, it is an opportunity to gain perspectives beyond what any single keynote or panel can offer, and to build relationships that will carry the ecosystem forward.

item.title: GTA 6 is rated 17+: What Indian parents should know before letting their children play
item.description: Graphic violence, nudity, sexual content and drug use feature in Grand Theft Auto VI's age-rating disclosures. As the highly anticipated game draws global attention, Indian parents face a familiar question: Should teenagers be allowed to play it?
item.content:encoded:
For Indian parents, the excitement around Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) comes with a significant caveat. The game carries an 18+ classification on Indian PlayStation and Xbox storefronts, while the US-based Entertainment Software Rating Board has rated it Mature 17+. In the UK and Europe, it carries a PEGI 18 classification.

The differences reflect regional rating systems, but the message is consistent: GTA 6 is intended for a mature audience, not children. Its content warnings have renewed a global debate about violence in video games, children's exposure to adult themes and the responsibility of parents in an increasingly digital entertainment environment.

What makes GTA 6 different?

Set in the fictional state of Leonida, with Vice City at its centre, GTA 6 follows protagonists Jason and Lucia through a world of organised crime, robberies and police pursuits.

The open-world format gives players considerable freedom to interact with the virtual environment, including civilians and law enforcement officers. Its age-rating disclosures flag intense violence, blood, graphic injuries, nudity, sexual activity, drug and alcohol use, strong profanity and adult humour.

The PEGI classification also identifies frequent realistic violence, graphic injuries and prominent drug references. This makes GTA 6 fundamentally different from games designed for younger audiences.

Why are child-safety experts concerned?

The concerns extend beyond children playing the game themselves. Gameplay videos, livestreams and social media clips can expose younger audiences to scenes from GTA 6, even if they do not own it.

Guernsey Police's digital safety lead Laura Simpson has reportedly warned parents about the game's depictions of blood, violence, decapitations and unhealthy relationships. Guernsey is an island roighly 113 kilometre south of England.

Psychologist Nicholas Kardaras, speaking to ABC News, has also cautioned that parents may underestimate the intensity and realism of violence in the franchise. Parenting expert Catherine Hickem has highlighted the importance of considering a teenager's emotional maturity before allowing access to adult-oriented entertainment.

However, exposure to fictional violence does not automatically translate into aggressive behaviour. Research on violent video games has produced mixed findings, and there is no established evidence that playing such games inevitably makes children violent.

The concern is whether younger players can process the content appropriately and distinguish between virtual entertainment and real-world consequences.

Can violent games influence children's behaviour?

Younger teenagers may not have the emotional maturity to interpret graphic violence, sexualised behaviour and substance use in the same way as adults.

Parents should watch for changes such as aggressive language, imitating inappropriate behaviour, increased irritability or withdrawing from activities outside gaming. The more important question is whether exposure to mature content affects a child's behaviour and everyday interactions.

Is GTA 6 addictive?

GTA 6's expansive open world, missions and side activities can encourage extended gaming sessions. For some teenagers, this could make it difficult to disengage.

Parents should look for signs that gaming is interfering with sleep, academic performance, hobbies or family interactions. Irritability when asked to stop playing and an inability to follow agreed screen-time limits are also warning signs.

The focus should be on whether gaming is affecting a child's everyday routine rather than simply counting hours spent in front of a screen.

Does GTA 6 have online interactions?

At launch, GTA 6 is listed as a single-player experience, allowing players to follow its storyline independently rather than interact with other players through an online multiplayer mode.

However, children can still encounter GTA-related content through YouTube, livestreams and social media. The PlayStation India listing also identifies optional in-game purchases, making it important for parents to review account permissions and restrict unauthorised transactions.

What should parents do?

The game's age classification should be the starting point for any decision. With an 18+ rating on Indian storefronts, parents should take its content warnings seriously, particularly when considering access for younger teenagers.

They should review the official content descriptors and gameplay footage to understand what the game depicts. PlayStation and Xbox offer parental controls to restrict age-inappropriate games, manage screen time and limit purchases.

For older teenagers, conversations about violence, criminal behaviour, substance use and the difference between fiction and reality are equally important. Parents should also monitor changes in sleep, academic performance and behaviour.

Should parents allow GTA 6?

GTA 6's popularity means children may encounter its characters and gameplay even without owning a copy. But popularity should not determine whether a child gets access.

Its 18+ Indian classification and extensive content warnings indicate that it is intended for adults. Parents of younger teenagers should be cautious about allowing access, while decisions involving older teenagers should take their maturity and ability to understand the distinction between virtual entertainment and real-world behaviour into account.

Ultimately, parental involvement must go beyond setting screen-time limits. Understanding what children play, what they watch and how they respond to it is just as important.

item.title: UPI was never free. But is its new merchant fee fair?
item.description: UPI's new MDR brings the cost of digital payments into focus. But questions remain over how the revenue will be distributed, whether smaller merchants and consumers will bear the burden, and if the framework adequately addresses competition and transparency in India's digital payments ecosystem.
item.content:encoded:
Should UPI be free? Any network that moves trillions of rupees a month needs funding. The real question is who pays and how.

UPI was never free. For six years the government paid through subsidies, banks through their technology budgets and depositors through lower interest on their savings. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra put it well: “It is not free even now; someone is paying for it.” The new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) makes that cost visible.

UPI processed over 24,000 crore transactions worth about Rs 314 lakh crore ($3.31 trillion) in FY26, and 14,500 crore worth Rs 177 lakh crore ($1.86 trillion) between April and September 2026. UPI handles about half the world’s real-time payments by volume, according to the IMF. Bank of International settlements (BIS) in July, mentions that fast payment systems with zero user fees and mandatory participation grow quickly, but the private firms that run them are challenged for want of revenue.

Comparing to some of the international payment systems- at 0.4% on payments above Rs 2,000, UPI’s MDR is below Indonesia’s QRIS (0.7% for larger merchants) and Chinese wallets (about 0.6%), close to Brazil’s Pix (roughly 0.22–0.33%), and a fraction of what cards cost.  In India, vendors receiving up to Rs 1 lakh a month pay no charges and railways, fuel, utilities and insurance pay a flat Rs 5.

India's charge is free up to Rs 2,000 ($21) which is about four times Indonesia’s. As per NPCI over 96% of merchant transactions by count stay free.  In this, a merchant receiving Rs 75,000 by NEFT pays nothing; by UPI, the same receipt would cost Rs 300 plus GST.

Merchant UPI payments in August 26, came to about Rs 8.95 lakh crore ($94 billion), of which about Rs 6 lakh crore ($63 billion) was above Rs 2,000. Allowing for the sectors which has flat Rs 5 as charges and the cap, the effective rate is roughly about 0.15–0.20%, which roughly gives a pool of Rs 12,500 crore ($1.32 billion) a year. Under the present formula, issuer banks take 40%, acquirers 30%, apps 20% and payer PSPs, the sponsor banks that connect apps to UPI, 10%. Banks could end up with as much as 60 to 70%.

Today, PhonePe and Google Pay hold about 80% of its user-facing market, as per the BIS bulletin. Together they would collect about Rs 2,100 crore ($221 million) a year. The BIS state that once a market has moved towards a few players, interoperability alone may not bring back the distribution to an even level... NPCI announced a 30% volume cap on any single app- in November 2020, but this has been deferred three times and is still not enforced six years on as tough to move the customers away.  

An IMF note adds that payments give large technology firms steady income and data to cross-sell credit and other services. This fee, which is meant to cover the cost incurred, would end up financing the two leaders’ wider ambitions. The other aspect is GST which at 18% applies to only the MDR and not to the total payment amount.  At the max cap, the merchant pays ₹354. Registered merchants claim it back as input credit. The real cost is for those merchants who cannot claim it back – (like composition dealers and merchants who sell exempt goods.

The passing of the charge  to the customer, will not stop merchants raising prices, so the buyer of a Rs 500 charger may end up paying for the Rs 50,000 phone. And charging even Rs 5 on one-off loan repayments above Rs 2,000, after years of moving microfinance borrowers away from  cash, is a retrograde step. The surcharge ban won’t stop shops raising prices instead, so the buyer of a Rs 500 charger quietly helps pay for the Rs 50,000 phone.

Suggestions:

Let the fee be fixed at Rs 100 for now, (pre-2020), and reset it every two years on audited cost data, a la US Federal Reserve does for debit cards. BIS says that such data is not available now and the Banks and NPCI should fix this immediately.

Let RBI, not NPCI, set the rate, as it does for debit cards, NEFT and RTGS. NPCI is owned by the banks that collect most of the fee.

Reduce the app share as volumes rise, so the largest players earn less per transaction, and let RBI set the tiers after public consultation. Unlike a volume cap, a taper works through price.

Publish each year who received how much payment.

Drop the Rs 5 on loan repayments. A repayment is not a purchase.

Hold acquiring banks answerable for surcharges and raise the Rs 2,000 and Rs 1 lakh limits with inflation.

NPCI has deferred the rollout past Diwali, and a public interest petition is pending in the Supreme Court. Use the time to fix the design rather than reopen whether a charge should exist. UPI won the trust of hundreds of millions of Indians because it was simple and fair. Its price must meet the same test.

(Sriram Kalyanaraman, Partner – BFSI and Advisor, Practus)

item.title: 7 Bryan Johnson longevity habits anyone can afford
item.description: Explore seven affordable longevity habits inspired by Bryan Johnson, from better sleep and daily exercise to balanced eating and stress management.
item.content:encoded:
Bryan Johnson has become one of the most talked-about names in the world of longevity.

The tech entrepreneur is known for Blueprint, an intensive health programme that uses medical testing, strict routines, specialised treatments and a carefully planned diet to study the ageing process.

His approach may involve expensive equipment, supplements and professional support, but not every habit in his routine requires a large budget. In fact, some of his most repeated recommendations focus on everyday choices such as getting enough sleep, exercising regularly and eating nutritious food.

For anyone interested in healthy ageing, the useful takeaway is not to copy his entire routine. It is to identify the simple habits that can fit into an ordinary lifestyle.

7 Affordable longevity habits inspired by Johnson's approach

1. Make quality sleep a priority

Johnson considers sleep one of the foundations of his health routine. He follows a consistent bedtime and aims to get around eight hours of sleep. His approach highlights an important habit that does not require expensive products or technology.

Try going to bed and waking up at roughly the same time every day. Keep your bedroom comfortable, reduce bright lights before bedtime and avoid scrolling on your phone when you should be winding down. Reading a book or listening to calming music can also help you establish a relaxing night-time routine.

2. Eat more whole foods

Johnson's diet places considerable emphasis on vegetables, berries, nuts, seeds and legumes. While his personalised meal plan is not necessary for everyone, the broader principle of choosing nutrient-rich foods is practical. Include seasonal fruits, vegetables, lentils, beans and whole grains in your meals.

Choose home-cooked food more often and reduce your dependence on heavily processed snacks and sugary drinks. These changes can be adapted to different budgets and food preferences without buying specialised longevity products.

3. Exercise regularly instead of chasing expensive treatments

Johnson combines strength training, cardio, flexibility and balance exercises in his fitness routine. However, building an active lifestyle does not require a personal trainer or an expensive gym membership.

Walking, cycling, dancing and bodyweight exercises can all help you stay active. Include activities that strengthen your muscles and improve cardiovascular fitness. Start with manageable sessions and gradually increase your activity according to your fitness level.

4. Get natural morning light

Morning light is another part of Johnson's approach to supporting the body's internal clock, also known as the circadian rhythm. Natural daylight helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle and provides a simple way to establish a healthier daily routine.

Spend some time outdoors after waking up, whether you take a short walk, sit on your balcony or enjoy your morning tea near an open space. You do not need specialised light therapy equipment if natural daylight is available. Avoid looking directly at the sun and protect your skin when UV levels are high.

5 Books that help you become more consistent in life

5. Reduce screen time before bedtime

A healthy sleep routine is not just about the time you go to bed. It also involves preparing your mind and surroundings for rest. Johnson recommends switching off screens before bedtime and creating a calmer evening environment.

Try putting your phone away around an hour before sleeping. Turn off unnecessary notifications, reduce bright lighting and avoid work-related messages late at night. Replace late-night scrolling with reading, journaling or a relaxing activity that helps you disconnect from digital distractions.

6. Make time for relationships and social connections

Longevity is not only about food, exercise and sleep. Johnson also includes family, friendship and community among the habits that support a healthier life. Make an effort to stay connected with people who matter to you.

Spend time with family, meet friends regularly or participate in activities that help you build meaningful relationships. Even a simple conversation can make social connection a more intentional part of your routine.

7. Track your health and build consistency

Johnson uses extensive testing and health data to monitor his progress. Most people do not need advanced biological-age tests or expensive wearable devices to become more aware of their health. Start with simple observations. Pay attention to your sleep schedule, daily movement, energy levels and eating patterns.

You can use a notebook or a basic habit tracker to record your routine. For medical concerns, regular check-ups and advice from qualified healthcare professionals are more useful than relying on online trends or unverified tests.

Final thoughts

Bryan Johnson's longevity routine may look out of reach because of its expensive treatments, specialised equipment and extensive testing. However, many of the habits behind his approach are accessible to people with ordinary budgets.

Prioritising sleep, eating balanced meals, staying active, getting natural daylight and maintaining meaningful relationships are practical starting points.

These habits do not promise to reverse ageing or guarantee a longer life, but they can support better overall health. The real lesson is to focus on sustainable changes rather than chasing every new longevity trend. You do not need to spend millions to start taking better care of your health.

item.title: 5 Books from Bill Gates' latest reading list before 2026 end
item.description: Explore five books recommended by Bill Gates, covering science, history, personal growth, and big ideas worth exploring before 2026 ends.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Gates is known not only for building Microsoft but also for his curiosity about science, technology, history, and human behaviour. Through his reading recommendations, he regularly introduces readers to books that challenge conventional thinking and offer fresh perspectives on the world.

His reading lists are particularly interesting because they cover subjects beyond business and technology, including personal development, global challenges, and human relationships.

As of November 2026, five of Gates' notable book recommendations come from two sources: his July 2026 summer reading list and his September 2026 appearance on The Ezra Klein Show. Together, they cover fiction, artificial intelligence, financial history, and international development.

5 Books from Bill Gates' latest reading list before 2026 ends

1. The Correspondent, by Virginia Evans

This novel follows an older woman whose life unfolds through letters and correspondence. Through her exchanges with family, friends, and strangers, the story explores loneliness, relationships, regret, and the possibility of rebuilding connections.

It offers a reminder that communication can help people understand themselves and reconnect with others, even after difficult experiences.

2. Into the Wood Chipper, by Nicholas Enrich

Written by former USAID official Nicholas Enrich, this book examines the dismantling of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). It offers an insider's account of the decisions, institutional challenges, and consequences experienced by people working within the organisation.

The book explores public service, international development, and the impact political decisions can have on institutions and the communities they serve.

3. The Infinity Machine, by Sebastian Mallaby

This book explores the development of artificial intelligence through the story of Demis Hassabis and DeepMind. Sebastian Mallaby examines the scientific ambitions, breakthroughs, competition, and safety concerns that have shaped modern AI.

For readers interested in technology, innovation, and the future of artificial intelligence, the book provides insight into the people and decisions driving one of the biggest technological shifts of our time.

Tell Me What to Read

4. Culpability, by Bruce Holsinger

This novel centres on a family travelling in a self-driving vehicle when a serious accident takes place, leaving another person dead. The incident raises difficult questions about responsibility and accountability.

Who should be held responsible when technology is involved in a fatal accident? Is it the driver, the manufacturer, or the company behind the software?

The story explores the complicated relationship between artificial intelligence, human decisions, and moral responsibility. Gates appreciated how the novel handles these questions while maintaining an engaging storyline.

Also Read
Bill Gates' top 5 book recommendations for managers

5. 1929: Inside the Greatest Crash in Wall Street History—And How It Shattered a Nation, by Andrew Ross Sorkin

This nonfiction book examines the 1929 Wall Street crash and the events that contributed to one of the most significant financial crises in modern history.

Andrew Ross Sorkin explores the key individuals, financial decisions, and market conditions behind the collapse. The book also draws attention to the relationship between speculation and investing, showing how financial mistakes can have consequences far beyond the stock market.

Gates recommended it for its detailed research and the lessons it offers about understanding financial history to avoid repeating past mistakes.

Final thoughts

Bill Gates' recent book recommendations cover a wide range of subjects, from artificial intelligence and financial history to human relationships and public institutions.

What makes this selection interesting is that each book offers a different way to understand the world. Whether you enjoy fiction, business, technology, or history, these recommendations provide an opportunity to explore ideas beyond your usual reading interests.

If you are planning your reading list before 2026 ends, these five books are worth considering.

item.title: Content, AI, empowerment: test your business creativity with Edition 259 of our weekly quiz!
item.description: This insightful feature from YourStory tests and strengthens your business acumen! Here are 5 questions to kick off this 259th quiz. Ready?
item.content:encoded:
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 259th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.

What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?

Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

Q1: Customer workflow

Most enterprises have tools to store customer records and manage calls – but employees often connect this data manually, leading to missed tasks and delayed resolutions. How can this gap be filled?

Q2: Enterprise content

Every enterprise is becoming a content enterprise – but many companies face challenges in creating relevant content quickly, accurately and at scale. Where is the entrepreneurial opportunity here?

Q3: Hemp

Hemp is a hardy crop, with many uses in fibre, food and oil. How can this business opportunity be tapped while also delivering an uplifting social impact?

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

Q4: Learning disabilities

Awareness of learning disabilities due to neurological conditions is rising in India, yet access to specialist care remains uneven. How can better care be provided here?

Q5: Audio entertainment

A growing number of listeners expect a wide range of audio content for entertainment, including blockbusters and hyper-personalised experiences. How can technology help create such content at scale?

Answers!

Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!

A1: Customer workflow

Founded by Henry Dag, Cogover brings CRM, built-in calling, workflows, and AI agents into one environment. This helps ensure that a customer interaction leads to a visible, accountable next step.

Customers can extract relevant information from a conversation, propose a record update or prepare a task. Read more here about how Cogover’s selection for NetApp Excellerator creates an opportunity to connect with a broader enterprise data perspective.

A2: Enterprise content

Founded and led by Prabhu Narasimhan, Brahma AI combines enterprise content intelligence and management with AI creation capabilities. They span visual AI, digital humans, voice, and multilingual performance.

item.title: CII proposes 15 financial sector reforms to boost long-term growth ambitions
item.description: Industry body CII has proposed 15 financial sector reforms, including a permanent liquidity window for well-governed NBFCs and higher priority sector lending limits for renewable energy.
item.content:encoded:
In a bid to strengthen India's financial system for long-term growth ambitions, the industry body CII has proposed 15 financial sector reforms, including a permanent liquidity window for well-governed NBFCs and higher priority sector lending limits for renewable energy.

The recommendations come against the backdrop of the government's constitution of a High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat, announced in the Union Budget 2026-27.

The Committee has a six-month mandate to examine the long-term capital requirements of banks, development finance institutions, and NBFCs; review priority sector lending norms; prepare a roadmap for AI and digital adoption; and examine prudential regulations.

CII Director General Chandrajit Banerjee noted that the financial sector enters this phase from a position of strength, with healthy bank and NBFC balance sheets and a series of important measures by the government and regulators over the past year.

"The task now is to build a system that can finance an economy several times its present size by 2047. That requires deeper and longer-tenor pools of capital, credit that reaches the sectors that will drive growth, and regulation that keeps pace with how finance is delivered. Our recommendations are intended to take the current reform effort to its next stage," Banerjee said.

CII estimates that a $26.5 trillion economy by 2047 would require financial assets of nearly $106 trillion, compared with around $7 trillion at present. It said banking assets would need to grow 3-3.5 percentage points faster than nominal GDP.

The industry body also flagged the relatively shallow corporate bond market, which accounts for around 15 per cent of GDP in India, compared with 36 per cent in China and over 80 per cent in South Korea.

To advance the ongoing reform push to its next phase, CII has called for raising the priority sector lending limit for renewable energy projects from Rs 35 crore to Rs 80-100 crore per borrower and including circular economy activities such as recycling and battery reuse within the framework.

For NBFCs, CII has sought a permanent, rule-based liquidity and refinance window for well-governed entities, with access linked to compliance status, collateral standards and eligibility criteria.

It has also sought to reduce the threshold for NBFCs under the SARFAESI Act from Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1 lakh, bringing them on par with banks and housing finance companies.

Other proposals include access to Debt Recovery Tribunals, the Central Repository of Information on Large Credits and central fraud registries, subject to appropriate safeguards and reciprocal data-sharing obligations.

To deepen corporate bond markets, CII has recommended allowing pension funds, insurers and provident funds calibrated exposure to bonds rated below AA and longer-tenor instruments.

In the insurance sector, the industry body has called for restoring input tax credit for individual health and life insurance policies by making them zero-rated rather than exempt under GST.

Other recommendations include raising the voting rights cap in private banks from 26 per cent to up to 49 per cent with governance safeguards, and increasing the foreign investment limit in public sector banks from 20 per cent to 49 per cent to help them raise capital.

CII has also called for extending the Account Aggregator framework to public databases, including land records, eMandi transactions, NREGA records and ration card data, subject to consent safeguards.

For MSMEs, CII has recommended making insurance cover against risks such as fire, floods, machinery breakdown and business interruption a standard feature of government-guaranteed loans. It estimates the MSME credit gap at Rs 25-30 lakh crore.

The remaining proposals include rationalising investment limits for insurers and pension funds, finalising the climate finance taxonomy, improving regulatory predictability for NBFCs, deepening domestic institutional capital for private equity and venture capital, and permitting certified automated video-based KYC.

item.title: Noel Tata seeks Tata Sons board meet recordings
item.description: Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has written to Tata Sons seeking the audio and video recordings of the September 17 board meeting of the holding company of all Tata Group entities.
item.content:encoded:
Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata wrote to Tata Sons again on Friday, seeking the audio and video recordings of the September 17 board meeting of the holding company of all Tata Group entities.

In a letter addressed to Tata Sons company secretary Suprakash Mukhopadhyay, Noel has asserted his rights as a board member in seeking the recordings of the September 17 board meeting and also the nomination and remuneration committee (NRC) of the board, which asked N Chandrasekaran to reconsider his decision to step out of the race for reappointment as the Tata Sons chairman, according to sources.

The NRC reportedly met on September 3 and decided to ask Chandrasekaran to reconsider his decision not to make himself available for reappointment.

In the letter, Noel said that Venu Srinivasan, a nominee director of Tata Trusts on the Tata Sons board, should have recused himself from the reappointment issue because of a conflict of interest.

The letter discusses dealings between the company chaired by Srinivasan and another owned by Chandrasekaran's son, sources said, adding that this amounts to a conflict of interest.

According to media reports, there have been business dealings between Hanno Warehousing, run by Chandrasekaran's family members and TVS Group. Tata Sons has previously denied any conflict of interest in the matter and asserted that the matter was duly disclosed.

Tata Sons has denied the recordings to Noel earlier this month.

Noel's letter was sent on Friday evening, hours after a meeting of two Tata Trusts, in which decisions for making grants of over Rs 250 crore were made.

According to sources, all resolutions at the meetings of Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and Tata Education and Development Trust were passed unanimously, and there were no discussions on matters beyond the agenda.

Srinivasan and Vijay Singh, who have sided against Noel, are trustees of SDTT.

The next board meeting of Tata Sons is slated for November 26.

item.title: Karnataka CM to lead delegation to Japan to explore investments
item.description: Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar will lead a high-level state government delegation to Japan from November 23 to 25.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar will lead a high-level state government delegation to Japan from November 23 to 25 to strengthen Japanese investments in the state and study the country's urban development practices.

The delegation will visit Nagoya on November 23, Osaka on November 24 and Tokyo on November 25, focusing on industry meetings and urban development initiatives, according to an official press note issued on Friday.

Minister for Large and Medium Industries and Infrastructure Development M B Patil will accompany the Chief Minister and lead industry engagements, anchoring Karnataka's investment outreach in Japan and the Republic of Korea.

The delegation will include senior officials such as Greater Bengaluru Authority Chief Commissioner M Maheshwar Rao; Commerce and Industries Department Principal Secretary S Selvakumar; Commissioner for Industrial Development; Director of Industries and Commerce; and Invest Karnataka Forum CEO Khushboo Goel Chowdhary, along with officials from the CMO, GBA, and the Commerce and Industries Department.

During the visit, the Chief Minister and the Commerce and Industries Department team will meet senior representatives of leading Japanese corporations to understand their investment plans and present Karnataka's investment opportunities.

The industry engagements will continue until November 27, and the companies will be invited to participate in the Global Investors Meet 2027, organised by Invest Karnataka at Bengaluru Palace from April 20 to 22, 2027.

The meetings will cover sectors including automotive and electric vehicle components with Toyota and Panasonic Automotive Systems; speciality chemicals and advanced materials with Mitsubishi Chemical Group; pharmaceuticals with Takeda Pharmaceuticals; industrial automation with Yokogawa Electric; and manufacturing investments with Sumitomo Corporation, the release said.

The delegation will showcase the state's policy support, including the Aerospace and Defence Policy, additional capital subsidy of up to 20 per cent for investments in backward and priority taluks, the KIADB Digital Industrial Land Bank and single-window facilitation for investment proposals.

A meeting with the Executive Vice President of JETRO will also focus on strengthening institutional support for Japanese companies investing in Karnataka.

On the urban development front, the delegation, along with the Greater Bengaluru Authority, will study Japanese practices in waste management and waste-to-energy, urban planning, transport and transit planning, architecture and urban design.

Japan's cities are considered global benchmarks for planned, high-density and sustainable urban growth. The visits to Osaka and Tokyo will provide an opportunity to study how the country plans, builds and manages high-density urban centres.

Tokyo, one of the world's largest metropolitan areas, is a global reference for integrated transit and station-centred redevelopment, while Osaka, the commercial and industrial hub of western Japan, offers lessons in large-scale urban renewal and metropolitan planning.

The site visits and meetings will include a visit to Tokyo Midtown Roppongi with Nikken Sekkei, one of Japan's leading architecture and urban design firms.

The large-scale mixed-use development is a benchmark for redevelopment, transit-oriented development, land readjustment, mixed land use and urban green spaces, the note said.

The delegation will also meet with senior management at JFE Engineering Corporation's Tokyo headquarters to learn about its capabilities and key projects in waste management, waste-to-energy, and urban infrastructure.

item.title: Google announces $5M funding for IIT Kharagpur for advanced AI research
item.description: The funding will support the institute's researchers and students across three core pillars: advanced AI research, educational opportunities, and AI capacity building.
item.content:encoded:
Technology giant Google on Saturday said it will provide IIT Kharagpur with $5 million (about Rs 46 crore) to develop and accelerate advanced AI research.

Speaking on the 75th anniversary of IIT Kharagpur, Director Suman Chakraborty said the institute's alumnus and Google CEO Sundar Pichai has envisaged the funding support for applied AI research.

"Google is providing the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur) with $5 million in funding to help develop and accelerate advanced AI research, while cultivating India's next generation of scientific and technical talent," the company said in a blog.

The funding will support the institute's researchers and students across three core pillars: advanced AI research, educational opportunities, and AI capacity building.

Under advanced AI research, the fund will support efforts to tackle critical, real-world challenges by deploying AI for Indic languages, materials science, agriculture, and educational technology.

As part of educational opportunities, it will support expansion of AI training and curriculum development for students and faculty.

The fund will support the institute's AI frameworks and tooling to elevate the technological ecosystem across the campus.

"IIT Kharagpur is driving groundbreaking work in areas like Indic languages, agriculture, and education, and Google is excited to help accelerate this impact with a new partnership. Looking forward to seeing this collaboration shape the path for the next generation of students, just as IIT Kharagpur shaped my own," Pichai said.

He said India is increasingly at the forefront of innovation; programmes like this will help implement Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision that the benefits of AI reach everyone in India.

item.title: India ties for APAC’s highest phishing rate as employee awareness gaps emerge: Kaspersky
item.description: India and Indonesia share APAC's highest reported phishing rate, but the survey's 70% employee-awareness finding points to a broader weakness in business cyber resilience.
item.content:encoded:
Phishing is the most frequently reported cyber incident among businesses surveyed in Asia-Pacific, but the sharper warning for India is that attacks are exploiting weaknesses in employee awareness as well as technology. 

In a Kaspersky survey, 28% of Indian businesses said they had experienced phishing between March 2025 and March 2026. India shares the highest reported proportion with Indonesia, above the APAC average of 24%.

The survey covered 1,800 interviews across 18 countries, including 100 Indian respondents. 

In India, 21% reported attacks involving weak or stolen credentials, compared with 15% across APAC. Mass malware attacks were reported by 21%, against 18% regionally. Software vulnerability exploits were at 20%, slightly below APAC's 21%. 

Among APAC respondents whose organisations experienced cyber incidents, 33% said attackers sought sensitive business information and 32% identified customers’ personal data as a target during their most harmful incident.

One of the most striking findings concerns employee awareness. About 70% of Indian respondents said their organisations had experienced at least one cyberattack exploiting employees’ low IT security awareness. That matched Malaysia and was above the APAC average of 63%, though below Vietnam’s 75%.

This sits uneasily beside another survey result. Some 53% of Indian respondents described their organisation’s cybersecurity culture as high, meaning employees were well-educated in IT security and followed the rules. The remaining 47% rated it average, indicating that staff knew basic practices but did not always act on them. None selected the lowest category.

“A phishing email can look like any other message on a busy workday, from a supplier's invoice to a request from a colleague. Employees may know what phishing is, but recognising it in everyday communications can be a challenge,” said Adrian Hia, managing director for Asia Pacific at Kaspersky.

Hia argues that businesses should move beyond basic instruction and give staff repeated opportunities to practise identifying suspicious requests through simulated attacks.

The threat is also becoming more sophisticated. In an advisory issued on August 7, 2026, India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned of targeted attacks against Microsoft 365 environments using password-spraying, credential-stuffing, device-code phishing and stolen session tokens. 

Device-code phishing abuses a legitimate sign-in process to trick a user into authorising an attacker's access. The advisory also describes business email compromise, in which criminals take over or impersonate business email accounts to divert payments or obtain sensitive information.

India’s regulatory framework is evolving alongside these risks. CERT-In requires specified cyber incidents to be reported within six hours of being noticed and calls for ICT system logs to be retained securely for 180 days within India.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, notified in November 2025, provide for phased compliance and require organisations responsible for personal data to inform affected individuals without delay after a personal data breach. The Reserve Bank of India’s 2026 directions for commercial banks and non-bank payment operators also formalise controls around cyber resilience and digital payment security.

item.title: Design, data, delight: how to get your message across at tech business exhibitions
item.description: In this photo essay from BTS at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre, we showcase highlights from the exhibition halls along with insights for innovators.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) wrapped up its 29th annual edition this week at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre. See our BTS exhibition showcases from earlier editions in 2025 and 2024, and YourStory’s TechSparks exhibitors from 2026 and 2025.

Such leading global exhibitions bring together investors, business owners, industry experts, government, and academia. Innovators can present their ideas and attract financial support to develop their inventions, as well as learn how to improve their presentation, marketing and communication skills.

Exhibitions allow startups to assess their competition and potential partners, understand market trends, and identify opportunities to make their solutions better. Furthermore, displaying innovative solutions can motivate students, aspiring entrepreneurs, researchers, and other visitors to think creatively and develop their own ideas.

In this photo essay, we feature the BTS startups and tech firms Cloud Victor, WorkSuite, DPDPsuites.AI, Bramma, AIsphere, Inbound, Umber, DialGrid, SuperAgent, NuWare AI, Tyrios, IT Idol, and others. We also showcase booths and pavilions of other states such as Keralam, incubators (Jain LaunchPad, K-Heal), and countries like Germany and Denmark.

CloudVictor is a cloud technology and infrastructure management company specialising in helping businesses optimise, secure and scale their Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. It aims to help organisations reduce cloud expenditure, improve infrastructure performance, and strengthen security while ensuring business continuity.

Also Read
Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India

WorkSuite is an integrated enterprise management platform by MJC GlobalTech, designed to bring multiple business functions together within a unified digital ecosystem. The platform incorporates AI-powered capabilities such as lead qualification, candidate screening, automated interviews, and workflow management.

DPDP Suites is an AI-powered data privacy and regulatory compliance platform developed to help Indian organisations comply with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. One of its key features is an AI-powered agent which acts as a privacy assistant by identifying compliance gaps, assessing risks, and providing actionable insights.

Bramma is an AI-powered workplace intelligence solution developed by Glymph Technologies. It combines specialised room hardware, multilingual speech recognition and AI to interpret conversations taking place in meeting rooms and workplaces.

AIESPHERE is an AI-powered CareerTech platform to support professionals in navigating their career journeys. The platform focuses on helping individuals identify suitable career opportunities, understand emerging industry requirements, develop relevant skills, and explore global employment prospects by leveraging AI and automation.

Umber is a technology company offering Digital Asset as a Service (DAaaS), an infrastructure solution designed to simplify the management and delivery of digital assets across different environments. By providing centralised asset management and controlled content delivery, Umber aims to reduce technical complexity and make digital content management more reliable.

DialGrid is an AI-driven business communication platform that helps organisations manage and automate customer interactions through voice, chat and messaging solutions. Its AI capabilities can improve response times, reduce customer service workloads and create more personalised customer experiences. DialGrid is particularly relevant to call centres and customer support teams.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

NuWare Systems helps businesses modernise their technology infrastructure and accelerate digital transformation. Its experience across industries such as banking, financial services, retail, and healthcare positions it as a partner for organisations looking to adopt AI at an enterprise level.

TYRIOS is an integrated enterprise software platform developed by Repalogic, part of the Germany-headquartered Deepbyte Technology group. It helps businesses manage customer relationships, business operations, marketing activities, and organisational data through a modular digital platform.

IT IDOL Technologies is a CMMI Level 5-certified custom software company that helps startups and enterprises scale their digital products. By combining software engineering expertise with AI-driven solutions and cloud technologies, it helps organisations automate processes, improve business performance and build scalable digital products.

As shown in this photo essay, innovators can make an impression (and an impact) with attractive and innovative booth design. An eye-catching layout, creative branding, and attractive lighting help here, with clear displays of logo and key messages.

Live demonstrations and interactive experiences help showcase real-world applications. Interactive displays, VR/AR experiences, or hands-on activities enable visitors to experience the innovation rather than just read about it.

Young innovators need to master the communication of innovation by explaining key problems addressed, uniqueness and benefits of their solutions.  Simple language, visual infographics and concise presentations go a long way here.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

Having an engaging and knowledgeable team at the booth or pavilion is important, for welcoming questions and catalysing meaningful conversations. They need to be prepared to explain technical details, business potential and future possibilities.

Beyond the exhibition, exhibitors need to strengthen their networking and follow-up opportunities via brochures, business cards and QR codes. They should collect visitor enquiries and potential collaboration leads, and follow up with interested visitors after the exhibition.

As seen in this photo essay, it is not just exhibitors who compete with one another, but large exhibitions themselves who compete with other events across the country and overseas. BTS has completed 29 editions, but there are other large tech business conferences in India and abroad.

To differentiate itself, BTS has created a unique theme and identity. It develops a distinctive annual theme that reflects the exhibition's vision and purpose. It includes experiential demonstrations, breakthrough technologies, real-world solutions, and innovation challenges.

There are dedicated zones where visitors can experience emerging technologies. Bringing together diverse stakeholders creates meaningful collaborations. Facilitating structured B2B meetings and investor–innovator interactions helps create opportunities for partnerships, technology transfers, and joint ventures. Flagship programmes, startup pitch competitions, and hackathons take the momentum to the next level.

Memorable visitor experiences are strengthened by attractive and thematic art installations, local cultural performances, and messages on environmental sustainability that promote selfies and social media buzz. Finally, in this day and age, AI-powered visitor recommendations, digital navigation, and smart registration are indispensable in creating curated visitor journeys.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at BTS 2026.)

item.title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (November 20, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Friday, November 20, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.

Featured stories  

WeWork India bets on GCCs and managed offices to drive next phase of growth

WeWork India has reported a 30% growth in both revenue and EBITDA, while its digital products have crossed an annualised revenue run rate of Rs 100 crore. Speaking to YourStory, CEO and Managing Director Karan Virmani said the company’s managed offices business now contributes 25% to its overall business, with major clients including T-Mobile, JPMorgan and Amazon.

The company has also launched Rivet, a design-and-build vertical catering to businesses looking to expand from smaller workspaces to larger, customised offices.

Read more

PayNearby is building a network of women micro-entrepreneurs through Digital Naari

PayNearby, a fintech platform, is building a network of women micro-entrepreneurs through its Digital Naari initiative, launched in early 2024. The programme has onboarded over 3.5 lakh women across 15,000-plus PIN codes, of whom 75,000–80,000 are currently active. The women are trained to deliver more than 50 financial and digital services, including banking, insurance, credit, bill payments, telehealth and commerce solutions. Around 80% of those joining the programme are first-time entrepreneurs.

Read more

Women founders use AI and emerging technologies to address social challenges

Women entrepreneurs across India are leveraging artificial intelligence and emerging technologies to tackle challenges in education, healthcare, livelihoods and sustainability. Founders including Namya Mahajan of Rocket Learning, Darshana Joshi of VigyanShaala, Priyanjali Datta of Aaroogya AI Foundation and Safiya Husain of Karya are building solutions that use technology to improve access to early learning, STEM education, healthcare and digital employment.

Read more

Other news

Drip Capital to facilitate Rs 5,000 Cr in trade finance for Bihar's MSME exporters

Drip Capital, a global tech-enabled trade finance platform, has signed an MoU with the Department of Industries, Government of Bihar, to facilitate up to Rs 5,000 crore in trade finance over five years for MSME exporters in the state. The agreement was signed on the sidelines of an investor meet in Patna. The collateral-free financing will address MSMEs' working capital needs, with funds available within 24–48 hours. Through its digital underwriting model, the company aims to extend formal credit to small businesses that may lack banking histories or assets.

The partnership will also leverage Drip Capital's B2B cross-border trade platform to connect Bihar's manufacturers with domestic and international buyers. 

Kelly expands Bengaluru delivery centre to scale global workforce solutions

Global workforce strategy and solutions provider Kelly has expanded its delivery centre in Bengaluru to support the growing demand for its outsourcing, consulting, technology and workforce solutions worldwide. The new office, which opened on November 20, marks the next phase of the company's investments in international talent markets. Kelly currently employs over 400 team members in India, supporting more than 50 clients, and has been recognised as a Great Place to Work in India for seven consecutive years.

The Bengaluru team supports global clients across managed service provider, recruitment process outsourcing, and science, engineering, technology and telecom services. It also handles supply chain operations, recruitment delivery and corporate functions, including HR, legal, IT, finance and marketing. Kelly, which has operated in India since 2001, serves clients in more than 70 countries and 60 languages, with delivery centres in Malaysia, Hungary and Mexico.

redBus opens 20 engineering projects to developer community through redBus Labs

Online bus ticketing platform redBus has introduced redBus Labs, an initiative that makes nearly 20 software projects developed by its in-house engineering teams publicly accessible on GitHub. The projects, which address practical engineering challenges, span AI, software development, website performance, and automated testing. The initiative aims to give developers and students in India and globally an opportunity to explore, use and build upon these tools.

The projects include mkpro, an AI-powered coding assistant; Idlefy, which improves website performance by managing less urgent tasks; and Selewright, which simplifies automated website testing. Other tools include LEAP, which uses AI to automate website testing through simple instructions, and Ananta, designed for efficient data storage and retrieval. redBus said automation testing tools used internally have helped reduce software test execution time by at least 40%. Developers can access the repositories and contribute improvements through GitHub.

Capital One appoints Bharath Vasudevan as head of India operations

Capital One Financial Corporation has appointed Bharath Vasudevan as senior vice president and head of Capital One India. In his new role, Vasudevan will steer the company's India strategy and oversee operations spanning AI, machine learning, data science, and modern software engineering. The appointment underscores India's growing importance as a strategic hub for the financial services company's technology, innovation and global collaboration initiatives.

Vasudevan brings over 25 years of experience across technology solutioning, risk management, analytics and financial services. He returns to Capital One after nearly a decade at Capital One Services. Most recently, he served as the chief revenue officer at deeptech firm Trusting Social and held an executive leadership position in the Enterprise Risk Office at Bajaj Finserv. Capital One India has been an integral part of the company's global technology ecosystem since 2004, developing capabilities in AI, data science, machine learning, and software engineering to support millions of customers worldwide.

PeopleStrong unveils 10 AI-native products to transform enterprise HR

AI-first HR technology provider PeopleStrong has unveiled 10 AI-native products and capabilities at Xponential 2026, its flagship Human × AI Confluence. Built on its existing platform, the offerings introduce specialised AI agents across the human capital management lifecycle, moving HR technology beyond transactional systems and predefined workflows towards intelligent platforms that can understand organisational context and execute tasks. The portfolio covers conversational AI, HR and payroll, recruitment, onboarding, implementation support and workforce intelligence.

The new offerings include Jinie MAAX, a conversational interface connecting specialised AI agents; Blitz, an AI-native HR and payroll platform; Phoenix Payroll; and MAAX Studio, which allows customers to build their own AI agents. Other products are AI Co-Recruit, an onboarding agent; Career Hub & Skills; Workforce Planning; and Multi Country Payroll. PeopleStrong said its AI-driven engineering cycle has improved internal efficiency by over 40%. The company serves more than 650 enterprises and 2.2 million employees across 10 countries.

item.title: (Weekly funding roundup Nov 14-20) VC funding bounces back after record low last week
item.description: Venture capital funding in Indian startups saw a sharp rise this week, propped up by a couple of deals in the $50-million range.
item.content:encoded:
The Indian startup ecosystem heaved a sigh of relief this week with venture capital (VC) funding rising sharply after it touched the lowest point for the year till now in the previous week.

The total funding for the third week of November was $255 million across 22 deals. In contrast, the previous week saw funding of just $26 million, largely due to the impact of festival holidays.

The sharp rise in VC inflow is a welcome sign for the ecosystem. This week's investor bets were spread across diverse segments such as AI, retail, food brands, and spacetech.

Whille no deal topped $100 million, there were two transactions in the $50 million range. In the year so far, only 16 deals have crossed $100 million, revealing the challenges the startup ecosystem continues to face in raising capital.

However, despite the sharp rise in fund flow this week, there has not been a strong momentum overall. This is largely due to the near-absence of a strong AI narrative in the country. The startup ecosystem hopes for better days in the coming year.

Key transactions

Dreamteam, an AI native customer relationship management startup, raised $53 million from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest.

Value fashion retailer Style Union raised Rs 485 crore ($52.1 million approx.) from Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners.

Physical AI startup Humyn Labs raised $47 million from Accel, Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, Jump Trading LLC, Lighthouse Canton, and Trifecta Capital.

Semiconductor startup Bharat Semi raised $24 million from Info Edge, South Park Commons, IndusBridge Ventures, Micromax, Valour Capital, Gaingels, and angel investors.

Food brand Boba Bhai raised $18 million from Left Lane Capital, BIG Capital, and Titan Capital.

Robotics startup Botsync raised $11 million from IvyCap Ventures, Capital 2B, AppWorks, Iterative, AngelCentral, Genesis Alternative Ventures, and angel investor Nalin Advani.

Fatehpuria Hygiene, a trading, supply chain and fulfilment company, raised Rs 100 crore ($10.7 million approx.) led by investor Madhu Kela.

Spacetech startup SatSure raised Rs 60 crore ($6.4 million approx.) from Antariksh Venture Capital Fund.

Circular economy startup Recove Ventures raised Rs 56.25 crore ($6 million approx.) from Samara Capital, Capri Global, and family offices.

Fintech startup Olyv raised $6 million led by Nippon Life India AIF Management Limited.

item.title: Spacetech firm SatSure raises Rs 60 Cr from Antariksh fund
item.description: SatSure’s Rs 60 crore investment from India’s dedicated spacetech fund will support satellite development, AI capabilities and global expansion as the country’s private space industry continues to gather momentum.
item.content:encoded:
SatSure, an Earth-intelligence company that uses satellite data to inform business and government decisions, has secured Rs 60 crore from the Antariksh Venture Capital Fund (AVCF). The investment leads the first close of its Rs 200 crore Series B round.

AVCF is anchored by IN-SPACe, India’s space-sector promotion and authorisation agency, and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital, an investment subsidiary of the state-owned Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI).

The round comprises Rs 165 crore in new equity, Rs 25 crore in venture debt, a form of lending designed for high-growth companies, and Rs 10 crore in secondary transactions, or share sales by existing investors. It is expected to close by December 2026. SatSure said its institutional funding will then total Rs 427 crore, excluding grants.

The proceeds will advance optical imaging payloads, the instruments that capture satellite images, developed by subsidiary KaleidEO ahead of a planned 2027 flight, support satellites for India’s Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership (EO-PPP), scale Dhaarini and expand overseas operations. 

Dhaarini is SatSure’s Large Earth Observation Model, an artificial intelligence system designed to interpret satellite and geographic data. IN-SPACe awarded it a separate Rs 24.6 crore Technology Adoption Fund grant in June.

Founded in 2017, SatSure operates across the Earth-observation value chain. KaleidEO develops optical payloads and satellites, while SatSure converts imagery into analytics for banks, insurers, infrastructure operators and governments. 

The Bengaluru-based company said its SatSource service is embedded in the Reserve Bank of India’s Unified Lending Interface, a digital platform connecting lenders with data providers. Public-sector banks, including State Bank of India, use it to assess farm loans. SatSure has 24 banking and financial-services customers, including HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, which are also shareholders.

“The strategic value of the space economy lies not only in reaching orbit, but in what we can understand from it,” said chief executive and co-founder Prateep Basu. 

SVCL chief executive Arup Kumar said the investment reflected AVCF’s focus on companies that combine "indigenous orbital infrastructure with downstream decision intelligence”.

The investment comes as India’s private space industry expands following reforms in 2020, the Indian Space Policy 2023 and relaxed foreign-investment rules in 2024. The government counted approximately 440 registered space startups in August 2026. Its EO-PPP programme has selected a consortium including SatSure, Pixxel, Dhruva Space and PierSight to build a 12-satellite constellation by 2029, with planned investment exceeding Rs 1,200 crore.

Recent funding has also flowed into other segments. Pixxel raised $100 million in September 2026, led by Temasek and Seraphim, while launch company Skyroot Aerospace secured $60 million in May from investors including GIC, Sherpalo Ventures and BlackRock. Digantara raised $50 million in December 2025.

These investments point to a maturing industry in which capital is backing not just rockets and satellites, but also the data and intelligence infrastructure needed to turn spacetech into commercially useful services.

item.title: What parents should know about GTA 6; Bike taxis could return to Karnataka
item.description: GTA 6, which is rated 17+, is intended for a mature audience. Parents must understand the game's content before deciding whether to allow access. In other news, the Supreme Court has rejected the Karnataka government’s appeal to reinstate the ban on bike taxis.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

Bike taxis could soon be back in Karnataka. 

The Supreme Court has rejected the Karnataka government’s appeal seeking to reinstate the ban on bike-taxi services. It observed that bike taxis should be regulated rather than prohibited, recognising their affordability and convenience for commuters.

In other news, home services platform Urban Company has raised Rs 2,500 crore through a QIP from domestic and overseas investors, including HDFC Life, Bajaj Life Insurance, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and Dymon Asia. The proceeds will fund the supply ecosystem for its on-demand household help service, InstaHelp, along with brand marketing, technology, and acquisitions. 

Still on funding, Bengaluru-based SatSure—which uses satellite data to inform business and government decisions—has secured Rs 60 crore from Antariksh Venture Capital Fund, India’s sovereign spacetech fund. This investment forms part of the first close of its Rs 200 crore Series B round. It comes at a time when Karnataka is aiming to increase its share of the country’s aerospace and defence sector from 65% to 75%. 

Moving on, Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu believes the political shift in Washington can trigger a sharp U-turn on immigration policy, reviving demand in the US economy. “The demographic fuel tap for the bubble was shut for a period and now it may be turned back on,” he said on X. 

Lastly, India ties with Indonesia for APAC’s highest phishing rate as attacks exploit weaknesses in employee awareness, a survey by Kaspersky shows.
